text:
**Short answer: for most people, LiFePO4 (LFP) is the better choice.** Nearly every current power station uses it, and the sources I found agree on why.

## Where LiFePO4 wins

- **Cycle life:** LFP stations are typically rated for 3,000 to 6,000 cycles, versus roughly 500 to 800 for the NMC models in the comparisons. At one full cycle a day, that's about 8 years versus under 2 ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/), [OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)).
- **Safety when something fails:** In lab tests, LFP cells burned cooler and less violently. One test saw NMC peak at 731 °C versus 259 °C for LFP ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). LFP isn't fireproof, and in one overcharge test it reached thermal runaway sooner. Its failures were just milder ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). That's a plus for a unit kept indoors or in a vehicle.
- **Price:** One retailer's data shows a median of $0.55/Wh for LFP versus $0.95/Wh for NMC ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Per rated cycle, LFP is far cheaper.

## Where NMC wins

NMC cells hold more energy per pound. But in finished stations the gap shrinks a lot. One database found only about 10% difference in median Wh per pound ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). Another found the LFP Anker SOLIX C1000 is lighter per Wh than the NMC Goal Zero Yeti 1000 ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). Compare actual models rather than assuming the chemistry decides weight.

## Things that don't depend on chemistry

- **Cold weather:** Most stations, LFP and NMC alike, won't charge below 32°F. Check the manual for your model ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).
- **Cycle ratings:** Check the end point. "4,000 cycles to 70%" promises less than "3,000 to 80%."
- **Fit first:** Make sure the output and capacity actually run what you need.

## When NMC is fine

Use it rarely (a few outages or weekend trips a year), need the lightest possible unit, or already own a working one. In those cases cycle life rarely becomes the limit.
